sentences.text: Sinornithomimus was a small ornithomimid measuring 2.5 meters in length and weighing about 91 kilograms.
The only known species of this genus is S. dongi.
The hand structure of Sinornithomimus is similar to Archaeornithomimus, representing an intermediate position between the ornithomimosaur Harpymimus and more advanced ornithomimids.
The high number of nearly intact specimens makes Sinornithomimus the most completely known ornithomimid.
The initial discovery included at least fourteen skeletons, with nine being nearly complete and uncrushed.
The pristine condition of the bones suggests a catastrophic event killed all individuals in the find simultaneously and instantly.
The first remains of Sinornithomimus were found in 1997 and formally described in 2003 by Yoshitsugu Kobayashi and Lü Junchang.
Dong Zhiming uncovered the first Sinornithomimus fossils in 1997 as part of the Mongol Highland International Dinosaur Project.
The fossils of Sinornithomimus were found in what is now Asia.
A 2001 expedition discovered a herd of juvenile Sinornithomimus fossils in the Gobi Desert in western Inner Mongolia.
This later expedition found another herd of thirteen juveniles and subadults at the same site.
Gastroliths found in the stomach areas of fossil skeletons support the hypothesis that Sinornithomimus was a herbivore.
Fossil arrangements in bonebeds with similarly aged juveniles corroborate that this species was gregarious.
The increase in running ability with growth is supported by adults having relatively longer lower legs, indicating cursorial proportions.
Sinornithomimus belongs to the family Ornithomimidae.
Sinornithomimus is classified within the class Reptilia.
Sinornithomimus is classified as a basal ornithomimid possessing some plesiomorphic synapomorphies of ornithomimids.

Sinornithomimus lived during the Late Cretaceous, possibly younger than approximately 92 million years ago, specifically in the middle of the Cretaceous period during the Turonian stage between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago.

It is debated whether adults formed familial protective groups or if juvenile herds were left to fend for themselves while adults nested or brooded, and while it was initially considered more derived than Archaeornithomimus, later analyses reversed this view.
